And the country wasn't ready for that at this time. The Supreme Court wasn't ready for that. And Congress passed what was called the Defense of Marriage Act. I voted for it. In retrospect, my vote was wrong. But I voted for it because there were two parts to it. And one part I still think was correct. And that was if one state did it and it wasn't recognized nationally, other states didn't have to recognize it. It's the same theory that if Utah had polygamous marriages because it's a Mormon state, Arizona doesn't have to recognize polygamous marriages. And that was the same legal argument there that we didn't have to recognize it because Hawaii had thought it didn't have to be recognized in another state. And so I voted for it on that basis. Of course, I was, as we know, almost 20 years later, the US Supreme Court came out and said, no, it's the basic right of people who were married, and the rule of law, it's got to apply to everybody there. But in 1996, when I cast that vote, there was a lot of controversy, there were a lot of people who knew I was gay, who thought that was a mistake, and they were determined they were going to out me, so to speak.
